chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: The history of Turkey, understood as the history of the area now forming the territory of the Republic of Turkey, includes the history of both Anatolia (the Asian part of Turkey) and Eastern Thrace (the European part of Turkey). These two previously politically distinct regions came under control of the Roman Empire in the second century BC, eventually becoming the core of the Roman Byzantine Empire.

events.text: From the time when parts of what is now Turkey were conquered by the Seljuq dynasty, the history of Turkey spans the medieval history of the Seljuk Empire, the medieval to modern history of the Ottoman Empire, and the history of the Republic of Turkey since the 1920s.

chapters.narrative: The history of Turkey is understood as the history of the area now forming the territory of the Republic of Turkey [S1]. This includes the history of both Anatolia (the Asian part of Turkey) and Eastern Thrace (the European part of Turkey) [S1]. These two previously politically distinct regions came under control of the Roman Empire in the second century BC, eventually becoming the core of the Roman Byzantine Empire [S1]. From the time when parts of what is now Turkey were conquered by the Seljuq dynasty, the history spans the medieval history of the Seljuk Empire, the medieval to modern history of the Ottoman Empire, and the history of the Republic of Turkey since the 1920s [S1]. The available excerpts reflect only a single source's perspective [S1].

chapters.title: Prehistory and ancient history
chapters.summary: Present-day Turkey has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic period and contains some of the world's oldest Neolithic sites. Göbekli Tepe is close to 12,000 years old.

events.label: 9000 BC
events.text: The Urfa Man statue is dated c. 9000 BC, to the period of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, and is defined as "the oldest known naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a human".

events.label: 4500 BC
events.text: Troy's earliest layers go back to around 4500 BC.

events.label: 2000 BC
events.text: Anatolia's historical records start with clay tablets from approximately around 2000 BC that were found in modern-day Kültepe.

events.label: 750 BC
events.text: Around 750 BC, Phrygia had been established, with its two centers in Gordium and modern-day Kayseri.

events.label: 657 BC
events.text: Numerous important cities were founded by these colonists, such as Miletus, Ephesus, Smyrna and Byzantium, the latter founded by Greek colonists from Megara in 657 BC.

events.label: 6th c. BC
events.text: All of Thrace, and the native Thracian peoples were conquered by Darius the Great in the late 6th century BC, and were re-subjugated into the empire in 492 BC following Mardonius' campaign during the First Persian invasion of Greece.

events.label: 330 BC
events.text: Achaemenid Persian rule in Anatolia ended with the conquests of Alexander the Great, defeating Darius III between 334 and 330 BC.

events.label: 188 BC
events.text: The resulting  Treaty of Apamea in (188 BC) saw the Seleucids retreat from Anatolia.

events.label: 4th c.
events.text: In the early 4th century, Constantine the Great established a new administrative centre at Constantinople, and by the end of the 4th century the Roman empire split into two parts, the Eastern part with Constantinople as its capital, referred to by historians as the Byzantine Empire from the original name, Byzantium.
It co-existed in Anatolia with Palaians and Luwians, approximately between 1700 and 1200 BC.

chapters.narrative: Present-day Turkey has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic period and contains some of the world's oldest Neolithic sites, with Göbekli Tepe close to 12,000 years old [S2]. The Urfa Man statue is dated c. 9000 BC and is defined as the oldest known naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a human [S2]. Troy's earliest layers go back to around 4500 BC [S2]. Anatolia's historical records start with clay tablets from approximately around 2000 BC found in modern-day Kültepe [S2]. Phrygia had been established around 750 BC with centers in Gordium and modern-day Kayseri [S2]. Byzantium was founded by Greek colonists from Megara in 657 BC [S2].

chapters.title: Byzantine Period
chapters.summary: The Persian Achaemenid Empire fell to Alexander the Great in 334 BC, which led to increasing cultural homogeneity and Hellenization in the area. Following Alexander's death in 323 BC, Anatolia was subsequently divided into a number of small Hellenistic kingdoms, all of which became part of the Roman Republic by the mid-1st century BC.

events.label: 334 BC
events.text: The Persian Achaemenid Empire fell to Alexander the Great in 334 BC, which led to increasing cultural homogeneity and Hellenization in the area.

events.label: 323 BC
events.text: Following Alexander's death in 323 BC, Anatolia was subsequently divided into a number of small Hellenistic kingdoms, all of which became part of the Roman Republic by the mid-1st century BC.
In 324, Constantine I chose Byzantium to be the new capital of the Roman Empire, renaming it New Rome.

Following the death of Theodosius I in 395 and the permanent division of the Roman Empire between his two sons, the city, which would popularly come to be known as Constantinople became the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.

During the reign of Justinian I (r. 527–565), the empire reached its greatest extent after the fall of the west, re-conquering much of the historically Roman western Mediterranean coast, including Africa, Italy and Rome, which it held for two more centuries.

The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 exhausted the empire's resources, and during the early Muslim conquests of the 7th century, it lost its richest provinces, Egypt and Syria, to the Rashidun Caliphate.

events.label: 7th c.
events.text: Between the 3rd and 7th century AD, the Byzantines and the neighboring Sassanids frequently clashed over possession of Anatolia, which significantly exhausted both empires, thus laying the way open for the eventual Muslim conquests from both empires' respective south.
It then lost Africa to the Umayyads in 698, before the empire was rescued by the Isaurian dynasty.
The fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire in 1453 marked the end of the Byzantine Empire.
The Empire of Trebizond was conquered eight years later when its eponymous capital surrendered to Ottoman forces after it was besieged in 1461.

chapters.narrative: The Persian Achaemenid Empire fell to Alexander the Great in 334 BC, which led to increasing cultural homogeneity and Hellenization in the area [S3]. Following Alexander's death in 323 BC, Anatolia was divided into small Hellenistic kingdoms that became part of the Roman Republic by the mid-1st century BC [S3]. In 324, Constantine I chose Byzantium to be the new capital of the Roman Empire, renaming it New Rome, and following the death of Theodosius I in 395 it became the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire [S3]. The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 exhausted the empire's resources and it lost Egypt and Syria to the Rashidun Caliphate and later Africa to the Umayyads in 698 [S3]. The fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire in 1453 marked the end of the Byzantine Empire [S3]. The excerpts reflect a Roman/Byzantine-centered point of view [S3].

chapters.title: Early history of the Turks
chapters.summary: Historians generally agree that the first Turkic people lived in a region extending from Central Asia to Siberia. Historically they were established after the 6th century BC.

events.label: 6th c. BC
events.text: Historically they were established after the 6th century BC.

events.label: 200 BC
events.text: The earliest separate Turkic peoples appeared on the peripheries of the late Xiongnu confederation about 200 BC (contemporaneous with the Chinese Han Dynasty).

events.label: 5th c.
events.text: The Hun hordes of Attila, who invaded and conquered much of Europe in the 5th century AD, may have been Turkic and descendants of the Xiongnu.

events.label: 6th c.
events.text: In the 6th century, 400 years after the collapse of northern Xiongnu power in Inner Asia, leadership of the Turkic peoples was taken over by the Göktürks.
From 552 to 745, Göktürk leadership united the nomadic Turkic tribes into the Göktürk Empire.
The Tang Empire conquered the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630 and the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657 in a series of military campaigns.
However, in 681 the khanate was revived.

chapters.narrative: Historians generally agree that the first Turkic people lived in a region extending from Central Asia to Siberia [S4]. Historically they were established after the 6th century BC [S4]. The earliest separate Turkic peoples appeared on the peripheries of the late Xiongnu confederation about 200 BC, contemporaneous with the Chinese Han Dynasty [S4]. In the 6th century, 400 years after the collapse of northern Xiongnu power in Inner Asia, leadership of the Turkic peoples was taken over by the Göktürks [S4]. From 552 to 745, Göktürk leadership united the nomadic Turkic tribes into the Göktürk Empire [S4]. The Tang Empire conquered the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630 and the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657 in a series of military campaigns, however in 681 the khanate was revived [S4].

chapters.title: Seljuk Empire
chapters.summary: The Seljuq Turkmens created a medieval empire that controlled a vast area stretching from the Hindu Kush to eastern Anatolia and from Central Asia to the Persian Gulf. From their homelands near the Aral Sea, the Seljuqs advanced first into Khorasan and then into mainland Persia before eventually conquering eastern Anatolia.

events.text: The Seljuq/Seljuk empire was founded by Tughril Beg (1016–1063) in 1037.

chapters.narrative: The provided excerpts describe that the Seljuq Turkmens created a medieval empire that controlled a vast area stretching from the Hindu Kush to eastern Anatolia and from Central Asia to the Persian Gulf [S5]. The excerpts also describe that from their homelands near the Aral Sea, the Seljuqs advanced first into Khorasan and then into mainland Persia before eventually conquering eastern Anatolia [S5]. According to the excerpts, the Seljuq empire was founded by Tughril Beg in 1037 [S5]. The excerpts note that Tughril Beg lived from 1016 to 1063 [S5]. The excerpts reflect only the information provided in the single source [S5].

chapters.title: Ottoman Empire
chapters.summary: The Ottoman beylik's first capital was located in Bursa in 1326. Edirne which was conquered in 1361 was the next capital city.

events.text: The Ottoman beylik's first capital was located in Bursa in 1326.
Edirne which was conquered in 1361 was the next capital city.
After largely expanding to Europe and Anatolia, in 1453, the Ottomans nearly completed the conquest of the Byzantine Empire by capturing its capital, Constantinople during the reign of Mehmed II.

In the Indian Ocean, the Ottoman navy frequently confronted Portuguese fleets in order to defend its traditional monopoly over the maritime trade routes between East Asia and Western Europe; these routes faced new competition with the Portuguese discovery of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488.

The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 marked the beginning of Ottoman territorial retreat; some territories were lost by the treaty: Austria received all of Hungary and Transylvania except the Banat; Venice obtained most of Dalmatia along with the Morea (the Peloponnesus peninsula in southern Greece); Poland recovered Podolia.
Throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, the Ottoman Empire continued losing its territories, including Greece, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and the Balkans in the 1912–1913 Balkan Wars.
The Ottoman Empire entered World War I (1914–1918) on the side of the Central Powers and was ultimately defeated.
On October 30, 1918, the Armistice of Mudros was signed, followed by the imposition of Treaty of Sèvres on August 10, 1920, by Allied Powers, which was never ratified.

events.label: 20th c.
events.text: Anatolia remained multi-ethnic until the early 20th century.

After largely expanding to Europe and Anatolia, in 1453, the Ottomans nearly completed the conquest of the Byzantine Empire by capturing its capital, Constantinople during the reign of Mehmed II [S6]. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 marked the beginning of Ottoman territorial retreat [S6]. chapters.title: Republic of Turkey
chapters.summary: The occupation of some parts of the country by the Allies in the aftermath of World War I prompted the establishment of the Turkish National Movement. The Turkish Provisional Government in Ankara, which had declared itself the legitimate government of the country on 23 April 1920, started to formalize the legal transition from the old Ottoman into the new Republican political system.

events.text: On 1 November 1922, the Turkish Parliament in Ankara formally abolished the sultanate, thus ending 623 years of monarchical Ottoman rule.

The Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923, which superseded the Treaty of Sèvres, led to the international recognition of the sovereignty of the new Turkish state as the successor state of the Ottoman Empire.
The abolition of the caliphate followed on 3 March 1924.
Atatürk's reforms caused discontent in some Kurdish and Zaza tribes leading to the Sheikh Said rebellion in 1925 and the Dersim rebellion in 1937.
Turkey was neutral in World War II (1939–45) but signed a treaty with Britain in October 1939 that said Britain would defend Turkey if Germany attacked it.
The Turkish leaders conferred with Roosevelt and Churchill at the Cairo Conference in November, 1943, and promised to enter the war.
The Turkish democracy was interrupted by military coups d'état in 1960, 1971 and 1980.

Following a decade of intercommunal violence on the island of Cyprus and the Greek military coup of July 1974, overthrowing President Makarios and installing Nikos Sampson as a dictator, Turkey invaded the Republic of Cyprus in 1974.
In April 2017, the constitutional amendments, which significantly increased the powers of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, were narrowly accepted in the constitutional referendum.
In June 2018, President Erdoğan  was re-elected for a new five-year term in the first round of the presidential election.
